textos.83706479-3535-4026-b2c1-e17df3a51419#963:
You can define fields by specifying a field name, a data type, and a field width. When you create a table, you need to define the fields that the table contains. [[T0]] tables can contain up to 255 fields.

> **Note:** If one or more fields can store null values, the maximum number of fields is reduced from 255 to 254.

The following list describes the general attributes you specify when creating a field:
 - Name of the field.
- Type of data that the field contains.
- Width of the field.
- Number of decimal places if the field contains numeric or float values.
- An index on the field.
- Whether the field accepts null values.

You can also perform the following tasks when working with fields:
 - Specify default values for the field.
- Add comments for the field.
- Specify input masks for entering and storing data in the field.
- Set automatically incrementing values in fields.

The following sections describes considerations when creating fields:
 - Considerations for Choosing Field Names
- Considerations for Choosing Data Types
- Considerations for Default Values in Fields

For database fields, [[T0]] stores the first 10 characters of the field name in the table (.dbf) file and the long name for the field in the database (.dbc) file. The rules for creating long field names are the same as those for creating any [[T1]] identifier except that database field names can contain up to 128 characters. For more information, see Creating [[T2]] Names.

However, as long as a table is associated with a database, you must use the long field names to refer to table fields, not the 10-character field names. If you remove a table from a database, the long names for the fields are lost, and you must use the 10-character field names stored in the table (.dbf) file as the field names.

If the first 10 characters in the long name are not unique in the table, [[T3]] generates a field name consisting of the first n characters in the long name appended by a sequential number for a total of 10 characters. The following table lists examples of generated names.

| Long name | Short name |
| --- | --- |
| customer_contact_name | customer_c |
| customer_contact_address | customer_2 |
| customer_contact_city | customer_3 |
| ... | ... |
| customer_contact_fax | customer11 |

In indexes, long field names can consist of characters, but not numbers. However, if you create an index using long field names and then remove the referenced table from the database, the index no longer functions correctly. In this case, you can shorten the field names in the index and then rebuild the index, or you can delete the index and recreate it using short field names. For more information, see Working with Table Indexes.

For more information about choosing field names, see How to: Name Fields.

When you choose the data type for a field, remember the following considerations:
 - The types of values the field can store. For example, you cannot store text in a numeric field.
- The amount of storage the field needs to store values. For example, any value with Currency type uses 8 bytes of storage.
- The types of operations you want to perform on values in the field. For example, [[T0]] can calculate the sum of values with Numeric or Currency type but not the sum of values with Character or General type. Tip For numbers that you do not intend to use for mathematical calculations, for example, phone numbers, use the Character , not Numeric , type.
- The capability to index or sort values in the field. For example, you cannot sort or create an index for fields with Memo or General type.

For more information about [[T1]] data types, see [[T2]] Data and Field Types. For more information about choosing data types for fields, see How to: Choose Data Types.

Specifying default values for fields help application users enter data more quickly by making it possible to skip fields unless they want to change the default value.

> **Tip:** If a business rule for your application requires that a field contain an entry, providing a default value helps to comply with that rule using a field-level or record-level rule.

For example, suppose a company has primarily domestic customers. On the form used to enter data for new customers, you might want to display the country for those customers as the default value in the country or region field. If other values are required for the country or region, the user can replace the default value with the appropriate value.

You can specify default values that are scalar values, such as a number, or expressions that evaluate to a scalar quantity. You can also specify any valid [[T0]] expression that returns a value consistent with the data type for the field.

> **Note:** When specifying the default value, [[T0]] evaluates the default value or expression for the correct data type when the closing the table structure or using the [[T1]] or [[T2]] commands. If the data type of the expression does not match the data type of the field, [[T3]] generates an error. Expressions that are user-defined functions ([[T4]]) or contain UDFs are not evaluated; and therefore, do not generate errors.

[[T5]] evaluates the default value or expression when using the [[T6]], [[T7]], or [[T8]] commands to assign values to fields. When you assign values to fields using the [[T9]] or [[T10]] commands, [[T11]] applies default values to any fields that are not explicitly assigned. However, these two commands do not replace any existing values with default values.

You can also use default values to populate fields that do not accept null values. When you add a new record, [[T12]] applies the default values then checks each field in the order they are defined for missing data. This makes sure that fields that do not accept null values can be populated with default values before applying the constraint that the fields cannot be null.

If fields in your tables accept null values, you can use the null value ([[T0]]) as the default value. Regardless of whether [[T1]] is on or off, if you use null ([[T2]]) as the default value, [[T3]] inserts null ([[T4]]) into fields for all commands except [[T5]]. For more information, see [[T6]] Command and How to: Permit Null Values in Fields.

If you do not specify a default value, a blank value appropriate for the data type of the field is inserted unless the [[T7]] command is set to [[T8]]. This preserves backward compatibility.

> **Note:** When you remove or delete a table from a database, all the default values for fields in that table are deleted from the database. However, stored procedures referenced by the removed or deleted default value remain even after the default value has been removed.

For more information about setting default values for fields, see How to: Create Default Field Values.

Specifies which records [[T0]] acts on in the current table or view. This dialog box appears when you choose Scope from the Export Options Dialog Box.
 **All**
The action affects all records in the table or view.
**Next**
The action affects a range of records beginning with the current record and continuing for the number of records you specify. Type a value of 1 to act on the current record.
**Record**
The action affects only the specified record number.
**Rest**
The action affects a range of records beginning with the current record and ending with the last record in the table or view.

This tab in the Combo Box builder controls column width and display.
 **Adjust the Width of the Combo Box to Display All Columns**
Specifies that all selected columns will display even if the open combo box must extend beyond the form boundary. This controls the Width property of the combo box.
**Column Grid**
Controls the values in the ColumnWidths property. You can adjust the column width by dragging the right edge of a column heading with the mouse. Double-click a column heading to hide the column. The grid shows actual data if it is available. If no data is available, the grid displays a message to that effect. To change column order, return to the List Items tab, remove the fields, and add them back in the desired order.

- Style Tab, Combo Box Builder

textos.83a38ddf-a8b9-4a8e-8057-99edbd55c3a2#964: When you import worksheet data, [[T0]] uses the first row in your Microsoft Excel worksheet to determine the data types of the fields in the new table. If the first row has literal text headings for each column, all the fields in the table will be character fields, even if the rest of the rows contain numeric data.

**[[T0]] FieldList**
Specifies the fields that appear in the Edit window. The fields are displayed in the order specified in FieldList . You can include fields from other related tables in the field list. When you include a field from a related table , preface the field name with its table alias and a period. If you omit [[T1]], all fields in the table are displayed in the order they appear in the table structure. The field list can specify any combination of fields or calculated fields, including fields from tables open in other work areas. The syntax of the field list is: FieldName1 [:R] [:[[T2]]] [:V = [[T3]] [:F] [:E = [[T4]]]] [:P = [[T5]]] [:B = [[T6]], [[T7]] [:F]] [:H = [[T8]]] [:W = [[T9]]] [, FieldName2 [:R]...]

The field list can contain statements for creating calculated fields. A calculated field contains read-only data created with an expression. This expression may take any form but it must be a valid [[T0]] expression.

The syntax of the statement you use to create a calculated field is:

CalculatedFieldName = [[T1]]

This example creates a calculated field called [[I0]]:

[[C0]]

The [[T2]] clause field list includes eight options, which enable special handling of fields displayed in the Edit window.
 **: [[T3]]**
Specifies the display size for a field in columns. The value of : [[T4]] doesn't affect the size of the field in the table; it alters only the way the field appears in the Edit window.
**:R**
In the following example, an Edit window is opened with the cust_id and company fields. The cust_id field is read-only and cannot be changed. [[T5]] ([[T6]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T7]] customer && Open customer table [[T8]] cust_id:R, company
**:V = [[T9]]**
Specifies a verify option that performs field-level data validation within the Edit window. If [[T10]] evaluates to true ([[T11]]) when you move the cursor from the field, the data input into the field is considered correct and the cursor moves to the next field. If [[T12]] evaluates to false ([[T13]]), the data input is considered incorrect, the cursor remains in the field and an error or exception is raised. If [[T14]] evaluates to 0, the data input is considered incorrect and the cursor remains in the field, but no error message is displayed. By default, [[T15]] is evaluated only when the field is modified. To force verification, include the :F option. You can display your own error message by including the :E option. The verify option isn't executed for memo fields.
**:F**
Specifies a forced validation option that determines if the expression in the verify option ( [[T16]] ) is evaluated when you move the cursor from a field or another window is activated. If :F is not included, [[T17]] is evaluated only if changes are made to the field. If :F is included, [[T18]] is evaluated, even if the field isn't modified.
**:E = [[T19]]**
Displays an error message specified with [[T20]] instead of the default system message. If the validation expression :V = [[T21]] evaluates to true ([[T22]]), the cursor leaves the field normally. If the expression evaluates to false ([[T23]]), the cursor remains in the field and the error message appears. If the validation expression :V = [[T24]] evaluates to 0, no message is displayed and the cursor remains in the field being validated. This lets you display your own error messages in validation routines. The error message is displayed only if [[T25]] is [[T26]]. The bell is sounded if [[T27]] is [[T28]]. The following example opens the products table and displays the product_id and prod_name fields. Enter a value greater than 100 in the product_id field to perform the field validation. :V specifies the validation criteria. :F forces the validation check to be performed whether the data is changed or not. :E replaces the [[T29]] system error message with a user-defined error message. In [[T30]], the error message is displayed in the status bar at the bottom of the main [[T31]] window. Press [[T32]] to close the Edit window. [[T33]] ([[T34]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T35]] products && Open products table [[T36]] _WINDOWS [[T37]] _MAC [[T38]] products [[T39]] in_stock :V = in_stock < 100 ; :F ; :E = 'The stock amount must be less than 100'
**:P = [[T40]]**
Specifies a picture option that lets you create an editing template specified with [[T41]] that controls the display and input of data for each field in an Edit window. For more information on using picture editing codes, see the Format Property and InputMask Property properties. The following example uses the picture option to allow only numeric data in a specific format to be entered in the unit_price field: [[T42]] ([[T43]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T44]] products && Open products table [[T45]] unit_price :P = '99,999.99'
**:B = [[T46]] , [[T47]] [:F]**
Specifies a set of boundaries between which data must fall. The boundary expressions [[T48]] and [[T49]] must match the data type of the field and cannot be the names of user-defined functions. If the data entered doesn't fall between [[T50]] and [[T51]] , a system message is displayed indicating the range between which the data must fall. By default, the data you enter is checked against the boundary values only if you make a change to the contents of the field. To force checking against the boundary values, include the forced validation option (:F). The following example ensures that the value in the in_stock field is between 1 and 100. Press [[T52]] to close the Edit window. [[T53]] ([[T54]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T55]] products && Open products table [[T56]] in_stock :B = 1, 100 :F
**:H = [[T57]]**
Specifies a heading option (:H) that allows you to replace the default field names with your own headings, which you specify with [[T58]] . By default, field names are placed to the left side of the fields in the Edit window. The following example provides user-defined headings for the displayed fields. [[T59]] ([[T60]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T61]] products && Open products table [[T62]] prod_name :H = 'Product Name:', ; unit_price :H = 'Price per Unit:'
**:W = [[T63]]**
Specifies a [[T64]] option that allows you to conditionally prohibit the cursor from being moved to a field based on the value of the logical expression [[T65]] . (:W) evaluates [[T66]] . If [[T67]] evaluates to false ([[T68]]), you can't move the cursor to the field. If [[T69]] evaluates to true ([[T70]]), you can move the cursor to the field. User-defined functions are supported in [[T71]] . Moving the cursor to all fields is prohibited if the current field is marked read-only. This occurs only when every field contains a [[T72]] clause that evaluates to false.
**Scope**
Specifies a range of records that are displayed in the Edit window. The scope clauses are: [[T73]], [[T74]] [[T75]] , [[T76]] [[T77]] , and [[T78]]. Commands that include Scope operate only on the table in the active work area. The default scope for [[T79]] is [[T80]] records. For more information, see the Scope Clauses online topic.
**[[T81]] [[T82]]**
Specifies that only the records that satisfy the logical condition [[T83]] are displayed in the Edit window. Using this argument allows you to filter out undesired records. Rushmore Query Optimization optimizes an [[T84]] query if [[T85]] is an optimizable expression. For best performance, use an optimizable expression in the [[T86]] clause. For more information, see [[T87]] Command and Using Rushmore Query Optimization to Speed Data Access .
**[[T88]] [[T89]]**
Specifies a condition whereby records are displayed in the Edit window for as long as the logical expression [[T90]] evaluates to true ([[T91]]).
**[[T92]] [[T93]] [, [[T94]] [, [[T95]] ]]**
Specifies the Edit window's font and font size. The character expression [[T96]] specifies the name of the font, and the numeric expression [[T97]] specifies the font size. You can specify a language script with [[T98]] . See the [[T99]] Function for a list of available language script values. For example, the following clause specifies 16-point Courier font for the fields displayed in an Edit window: [[T100]] 'Courier',16 If you include the [[T101]] clause but omit the font size [[T102]] , a 10-point font is used in the Edit window. If you omit the [[T103]] clause, 8-point [[T104]] Sans Serif is used. If the font you specify is not available, a font with similar font characteristics is substituted.
**[[T105]] [[T106]]**
Specifies the Edit window's font style in [[T107]]. If you omit the [[T108]] clause, the Normal font style is used. If the font style you specify is not available, a font style with similar characteristics is substituted. Character Font style B Bold I Italic N Normal O Outline Q Opaque S Shadow - Strikeout T Transparent U Underline You can include more than one character to specify a combination of font styles. The following example opens an Edit window and uses an underlined font: [[T109]] ([[T110]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T111]] customer && Opens customer table [[T112]] _WINDOWS [[T113]] contact [[T114]] 'System', 15 [[T115]] '[[T116]]' [[T117]] _MAC [[T118]] contact [[T119]] 'Geneva', 14 [[T120]] '[[T121]]' [[T122]]
**[[T123]] FieldName**
Allows changes to be made to only one field specified with FieldName in the Edit window. The remaining fields are displayed and cannot be edited.
**[[T124]] [[T125]] [, [[T126]] ]**
Limits the scope of records that are displayed in the Edit window. With [[T127]], you can specify an index key value ( [[T128]] ) or a range of key values ( [[T129]] , [[T130]] ) for the records displayed in the Edit window. The table must be indexed, and the index key value or values included in the [[T131]] clause must be the same data type as the index expression of the master index file or master tag. In the following example, only records with postal codes falling within the range of 10,000 to 30,000 are displayed in the Edit window: [[T132]] ([[T133]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T134]] customer && Open customer table [[T135]] postalcode [[T136]] '10000', '30000'
**[[T137]] | [[T138]]**
Saves any configuration changes made to the appearance of an Edit window. The changes are saved in the [[T139]] file and can include changes to the field list, the size of each field, and the location and size of the Edit window. For more information on this file, see [[T140]] Command . If you issue [[T141]] with the [[T142]] clause, the Edit window opens in the same configuration that was last saved in the [[T143]] file. This restores the previous Edit window configuration created with the last [[T144]]. If the last [[T145]] command issued in the Command window included a long list of clauses, issue [[T146]] to avoid having to retype the command. Any Edit window configuration changes you make in the current session aren't saved if you exit [[T147]] by pressing [[T148]]+Q.
**[[T149]]**
Places the cursor in the first field in the left partition of the Edit window. An Edit window can be split into left and right partitions by including the [[T150]] clause. By default, the cursor is placed in the first field in the right partition when the Edit window is opened. The cursor is placed in the right partition of the Edit window if you include [[T151]] without the [[T152]] clause.
**[[T153]] ObjectName**
Creates an object reference for the Edit window, allowing you to manipulate the Edit window with object-oriented properties available for the Grid control. For additional information about object-oriented programming in [[T154]], see Object-Oriented Programming . For additional information about the Grid control properties that you can specify for an Edit window created with the [[T155]] clause, see the Grid Control topic.
**[[T156]]**
Prevents the user from adding records to the table by pressing [[T157]]+Y or choosing Append Mode from the View menu. Note Including [[T158]] doesn't prevent you from appending a record from within a routine (created with [[T159]], [[T160]], or [[T161]]) while in the Edit window.
**[[T162]]**
Specifies to always use the field name of a table or view for the column headers, even when the database contains a friendly caption for the table. This clause applies only to tables or views in a database.
**[[T163]]**
Prevents records from being marked for deletion from within an Edit window. By default, a record can be marked for deletion by pressing [[T164]]+T, choosing Toggle Deletion Mark from the Table menu or clicking in the leftmost column of the record to be deleted. Note Including [[T165]] doesn't prevent you from marking a record for deletion from within a routine (created with [[T166]], [[T167]] or [[T168]]) while in the Edit window.
**[[T169]] | [[T170]]**
Prevents a user from modifying the table. [[T171]] and [[T172]] are identical. If you include either clause, you can browse or search the table, but you cannot edit it. However, you can append and delete records.
**[[T173]]**
Unlinks partitions in the Edit window. By default, the left and right partitions of the Edit window are linked; when you scroll through one partition, the other partition scrolls.
**[[T174]]**
Removes the Table menu title in [[T175]] from the system menu bar, preventing access to the Edit menu.
**[[T176]]**
Disables Rushmore Query Optimization of [[T177]]. For more information, see [[T178]] Command and Using Rushmore Query Optimization to Speed Data Access .
**[[T179]]**
Opens the Edit window with its normal default settings, such as its colors, size, position, title, and control options ([[T180]], [[T181]], [[T182]], and so on). If you omit [[T183]] and the current output window is a user-defined window with its own settings, the Edit window assumes those user-defined settings as well.
**[[T184]]**
Continues program execution immediately after the Edit window is opened. The program doesn't wait for the Edit window to be closed but continues executing on the program line immediately following the program line containing [[T185]]. If you omit [[T186]], when [[T187]] is issued from within a program, an Edit window is opened and program execution pauses until the Edit window is closed. [[T188]] is available only from within a program. Including [[T189]] when issuing [[T190]] from the Command window has no effect.
**[[T191]] [[T192]]**
Splits an Edit window into left and right partitions with [[T193]] specifying the column number of the split bar. For example, if [[T194]] is 20, the split bar is placed in column 20 of the Edit window.
**[[T195]]**
Specifies that the left partition of the Edit window appears in Browse mode.
**[[T196]]**
Specifies that the right partition of the Edit window appears in Browse mode. The following examples opens an Edit window with the split bar placed in column 20 and the right partition open in Browse mode. Include both keywords to open both partitions in Browse mode. [[T197]] ([[T198]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T199]] customer && Opens customer table [[T200]] 30 [[T201]]
**[[T202]] PreferenceName**
Saves an Edit window's attributes and options for later use. Unlike [[T203]], which restores the Edit window as it appeared in the previous session, [[T204]] saves an Edit window's attributes indefinitely in the [[T205]] resource file. Preferences can be retrieved at any time. For more information about the [[T206]] resource file, see [[T207]] Command . Issuing [[T208]] with the specified preference name PreferenceName for the first time creates an entry in the [[T209]] file that saves the Edit window configuration. Issuing [[T210]] later with the same preference name restores the Edit window to that preference state. When the Edit window is closed, the preference state is updated. Preference names can be up to 10 characters long, must begin with a letter or an underscore, and can contain any combination of letters, numbers, and underscores. Once you have a preference the way you like it, you can prevent it from being changed. Close the Edit window, issue [[T211]], open the [[T212]] file as a table, and change the field containing the preference to read-only by changing the value of the logical field [[T213]] to true ([[T214]]). For more information about the [[T215]] resource file, see [[T216]] Command .
**[[T217]]**
Prevents the record pointer from being moved from its current position to the top of the table. By default, [[T218]] positions the record pointer at the top of the table.
**[[T219]]**
Keeps the Edit window and any of its memo field text-editing windows active and visible (open). You can then return to the Edit window after cycling through other open windows with the keyboard or the mouse. [[T220]] is available only from within a program. [[T221]] has no effect when included with [[T222]] in the Command window because [[T223]] is always the default in the interactive mode.
**[[T224]] [[T225]]**
Specifies how long an Edit window waits for input. The numeric expression [[T226]] specifies how many seconds can elapse without any input before the Edit window automatically closes. [[T227]] is available only from within a program; it has no effect when you issue [[T228]] from the Command window. In the following example, the Edit window is closed if no input occurs in 10 seconds. [[T229]] [[T230]] [[T231]] 1,1 [[T232]] 24,40 ; [[T233]] ; [[T234]] ; [[T235]] 10 [[T236]] ([[T237]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T238]] customer && Open customer table [[T239]] [[T240]] ; [[T241]] phone :H = 'Phone Number:' , ; company :H = 'Company:' ; [[T242]] 10 [[T243]] [[T244]]
**[[T245]] [[T246]]**
Overrides the default table name or alias that appears in the Edit window title bar with the title you specify with [[T247]] . Otherwise, the name or alias of the table being browsed appears in the title bar. If you issue [[T248]] to place the Edit window in a user-defined window, the Edit window's title replaces the user-defined window's title. [[T249]] ([[T250]](2) + 'data\testdata') [[T251]] customer && Open customer table [[T252]]; [[T253]] 'My Edit Window' ; [[T254]] phone :H = 'Phone Number' , ; company :H = 'Company:'
**[[T255]] [[T256]]**
Performs record-level validation in an Edit window. The [[T257]] clause is executed only if a change is made to the record and you move the cursor to another record. The [[T258]] clause is not executed if the only change is to a memo field. If [[T259]] returns true ([[T260]]), you can move the cursor to another record. If [[T261]] returns false ([[T262]]), the cursor remains in the current field and [[T263]] displays an error message. You can display your own error message when [[T264]] returns false by including the [[T265]] clause. The character expression [[T266]] is displayed as the error message. If [[T267]] returns 0, the cursor remains in the current field, and an error message isn't displayed. The [[T268]] clause shouldn't be confused with the verify option (:V), which enables field-level validation.
**:F**
Forces the [[T269]] clause to execute before the user moves the cursor to the next record. In this case, [[T270]] is executed even if the record isn't changed.
**[[T271]] [[T272]]**
Specifies an error message that overrides the system default and whose contents you define with [[T273]] . [[T274]] displays your error message when [[T275]] returns false ([[T276]]).
**[[T277]] [[T278]]**
Evaluates a condition when the user moves the cursor to another record. If [[T279]] evaluates to true ([[T280]]), the user can modify the record moved to. If [[T281]] evaluates to false ([[T282]]) or 0, the record the user moves to becomes read-only and cannot be modified. The [[T283]] clause isn't executed when another window is activated.
**[[T284]] [[T285]]**
Limits the number of characters displayed for all fields in a partition of the Edit window to [[T286]] . Including the [[T287]] clause doesn't change the size of fields in the table itself; it alters only the way the fields are displayed in the Edit window. If a width has been specified for an individual field with the [[T288]] clause, it overrides the width specified with the [[T289]] clause for that field.
**[[T290]] WindowName1**
Specifies a user-defined window whose characteristics the Edit window assumes. For example, if the user-defined window is created with the [[T291]] clause, the Edit window can be moved. The specified window doesn't have to be active or visible, but it must be defined.
